newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Labour intensive S.African firms seen moving north.
newsitem.headline: Labour intensive S.African firms seen moving north.

text.p: A major shift in low-tech, labour intensive South African manufacturers to neighbouring countries in southern Africa is under way, Investec Securities research analyst Arnold Werbeloff said on Friday.

"The trend is not readily reversible and the choice clearly lies between moving upmarket or continuing to provide low value-added products but being undercut in the local market," he said in the latest issue of Clothing Industry News.

"The attitude of the South African government is to provide employment in the region so as to reduce the inflow of jobless immigrants, so we can expect further concessions to those who decide to take the regional option when relocating their plants."
Most affected would be the clothing, footwear, textiles, electronics and motor industries.
The major attractions of other Southern African Development Community (SADC) countries included lower wages, better incentives, labour stability and higher productivity.

For the clothing industry, the disincentives for staying in South Africa included high interest rates, the surge in illegal imports, still high tariffs on raw materials and import parity pricing by textile producers.
Werbeloff said clothing industries would also be "severely tempted" to relocate to other SADC states as trade barriers between them and South Africa came down, leading to a free trade area by 2004.
"The implications for investors are that when manufacturing operations move to SADC countries, control remains in South Africa and the profits are (usually) repatriated," he said.
Profitability was expected to increase, enhancing the prospects of companies that did make the move.
"This does not mean that companies which supply value-added products into local chain stores should move operations to neighbouring countries," he said.

"Such organisations recognise the impact of imported competition and their strategies include re-engineering, going upmarket, upgrading worker skills, sub-contracting to cut-make and trim producers throughout the region, developing electronic linkages to retailers, promoting exports and strengthening their design capabilities."
